content_units: Melbourne Dinner Fit at a Glance

For your group, the best cuisine choice is the one that clears   three constraints first  : enough vegetarian mains, safe gluten-handling, and a room that feels social without becoming shouty. On your budget of   about AUD 35 pp before drinks  , all four cuisines can work, but   Indian and Middle Eastern   are usually the easiest for mixed dietary needs,   Thai   can be great with careful sauce checks, and   Italian   is the most variable for gluten safety at this price point.
Thai vs Indian vs Middle Eastern vs Italian
Cuisine   Budget fit at  AUD 35 pp   Vegetarian depth   Gluten-free ease   Cross-contamination risk   Lively-not-too-noisy fit   Best use case
Thai   Good if sharing   Good   Moderate   Moderate to high from sauces, fryers, noodles   Often lively; noise varies a lot   Group likes share plates and bold flavours
Indian   Very good   Excellent   Good to very good   Moderate from breads, fryers, buffet/tandoor handling   Usually easier to find conversational rooms   Safest all-rounder for your group
Middle Eastern   Very good   Very good   Good   Moderate from pita, shared grills, fried items   Often warm and social without nightclub volume   Best balance of shareability and comfort

Italian   Moderate at this budget   Moderate to good   Variable   Moderate to high from pasta/pizza flour in kitchen   Can be ideal if more trattoria than packed wine bar   Best only if gluten handling is clearly strong
What to Order and What to Ask
Thai: best if you want sharing and bright flavours
- Usually works well for a six-person table because you can mix curries, stir-fries, rice, and veg sides.
- Biggest issue is that   gluten can hide in soy sauce, oyster sauce, fish sauce blends, curry pastes, and fried items  .
Good menu targets:
- Vegetable green curry or red curry with rice
- Tofu stir-fry using confirmed gluten-free sauce
- Papaya salad if dressing is checked
- Fresh rice paper rolls
- Jasmine rice, coconut rice, wok greens
Items to treat carefully:
- Pad Thai unless they confirm sauce ingredients and separate handling
- Fried tofu, spring rolls, tempura-style vegetables
- Satay sauces and marinades
- Anything labeled “crispy”
Questions for the kitchen:
- “Which sauces contain wheat or regular soy sauce?”
- “Can the gluten-free dish be made with   tamari or gluten-free soy  ?”
- “Are gluten-free noodles cooked in separate water?”
- “Is fried tofu or any GF item cooked in a   shared fryer   with battered foods?”
- “Do curry pastes or premade sauces contain gluten?”
Best sign it’s a fit:
- Staff can immediately explain which dishes are naturally gluten-free and which sauces can be swapped.
Indian: strongest all-round option
- Usually the easiest cuisine for   two vegetarians plus one gluten-avoidant guest   without making the rest of the table feel restricted.
- Strong value at your budget, especially if you share curries, rice, and a few sides.
Good menu targets:
- Chana masala
- Dal tadka or dal makhani
- Palak paneer or saag paneer
- Baingan bharta
- Vegetable jalfrezi
- Rice dishes, cucumber raita, salad
- Tandoori vegetables if marinade is checked
Items to treat carefully:
- Naan and breads for the gluten-avoidant guest
- Pakora or samosa if fried in shared oil
- Malai kofta if thickener is unclear
- Paneer dishes with creamy sauces if flour is used for body
- Anything from a buffet setup
Questions for the kitchen:
- “Which vegetarian curries are   naturally gluten-free  , not just modifiable?”
- “Do any sauces use flour as a thickener?”
- “Are pakoras/samosas fried in a   shared fryer  ?”
- “Can the gluten-free meal be served with rice instead of bread with no garnish contamination?”
- “Is the tandoor handling bread and gluten-free items in a way that could cause contact?”
Best sign it’s a fit:
- Several vegetarian mains are already GF or easily made GF without changing the whole dish.
Middle Eastern: best balance of sociable and manageable
- Great for a table that wants lively conversation, many plates, and flexible ordering.
- Usually easier to keep vegetarians happy than Italian, and often easier on gluten than Thai if you avoid bread-heavy spreads.
Good menu targets:
- Falafel if fryer is safe
- Mujadara
- Grilled halloumi
- Roasted cauliflower
- Fattoush without pita, if dressing is checked
- Eggplant dishes like baba ghanoush
- Lentil soups, rice, stuffed vegetables
- Mezze platters with GF substitutions
Items to treat carefully:
- Pita-served dishes
- Falafel from shared fryers
- Tabbouleh if any nonstandard grain is used beyond bulgur assumptions
- Kofta or skewers if marinades contain fillers
- Shared mezze platters where bread touches dips
Questions for the kitchen:
- “Can dips and mezze be served with   vegetable crudites or extra rice   instead of pita?”
- “Is falafel cooked in a   shared fryer  ?”
- “Does the dressing or marinade contain wheat, breadcrumbs, or malt vinegar?”
- “Can the gluten-free person have a separately plated portion before bread is placed on the table?”
- “Which vegetarian dishes are fully gluten-free without modification?”
Best sign it’s a fit:
- They can build a mezze spread with clear bread substitutions and separate plating.
Italian: choose only if the venue is explicitly good at dietary handling
- This can absolutely be enjoyable, but it is the   least reliable   of the four for your exact group at this budget unless the restaurant is known for gluten-free pasta/pizza protocols.
- Vegetarian options are common, but not always varied enough for two vegetarians unless the menu is broad.
Good menu targets:
- Gluten-free pasta with a simple tomato-based or vegetable sauce
- Risotto if stock and add-ins are checked
- Polenta-based dishes
- Caprese or burrata-style starters if suitable
- Wood-roasted vegetables, salads, mushroom dishes
Items to treat carefully:
- Pizza in flour-heavy kitchens
- Shared pasta water
- Arancini, crumbed eggplant, fried zucchini
- Gnocchi unless clearly gluten-free
- Cream sauces thickened with flour
Questions for the kitchen:
- “Is gluten-free pasta cooked in   separate water   with separate utensils?”
- “Is gluten-free pizza prepared away from airborne flour and baked on a separate tray?”
- “Do sauces or soups use flour?”
- “Are fried items cooked in a shared fryer?”
- “How many vegetarian mains are available beyond one pasta and one pizza?”
Best sign it’s a fit:
- They have a practiced gluten-free protocol, not just a token GF pasta note on the menu.
Group Decision Rules for This Specific Dinner
Best overall ranking
1.   Indian
2.   Middle Eastern
3.   Thai
4.   Italian
Why this order:
-   Indian   gives the best mix of vegetarian variety, gluten flexibility, and value.
-   Middle Eastern   is excellent for a sociable meal and usually lands in the sweet spot for energy level.
-   Thai   is fun and budget-friendly, but requires the most sauce and fryer checking.
-   Italian   can be lovely, but is the riskiest for flour exposure and limited vegetarian depth unless the venue is especially well set up.
Fast elimination checklist
Reject a venue if:
- It has only   1-2 vegetarian mains
- Staff sound vague about   shared fryers, sauce ingredients, or separate prep
- The menu forces the gluten-avoidant guest into just a salad
- Most value comes from bread, pizza, or noodle dishes with unclear GF handling
- Reviews or venue style suggest   bar-loud   rather than dining-room lively
What “lively but not too noisy” usually looks like
Pick places with:
- Dining room focus rather than bar focus
- Soft furnishings, booths, curtains, or smaller rooms
- Mid-evening service energy rather than late-night turnover
- Shared plates or curries rather than loud sports/bar screening vibes
Shortlist Strategy for Booking
Option 1: Indian dinner spot   Best all-round fit for vegetarians, gluten flexibility, and budget   Lowest-friction choice
Check menus
Option 2: Middle Eastern mezze venue   Best for a social table and moderate noise   Strong second choice
Compare options
Option 3: Thai with clear GF notes   Great if the menu labels sauces and fryer practices clearly   Higher diligence needed
Read reviews
